concept: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k elements that appear most frequently. The answer may be returned in any order. It is guaranteed that the answer is unique.

solutions.label: Sort by Frequency
solutions.summary: Count every element's frequency using a hash map, then sort all unique elements by their frequency in descending order and return the first k.

solutions.label: Heap-Based Selection
solutions.summary: Count frequencies with a hash map, then maintain a min-heap of size k. For each unique element, push it onto the heap and pop the smallest when the heap exceeds size k. The heap retains the top k frequent elements.

solutions.label: Bucket Sort
solutions.summary: Count frequencies with a hash map, then create an array of buckets where index i holds elements that appear exactly i times. Walk the bucket array from the highest index downward, collecting elements until k are gathered.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Alright, let's jump into the next problem. You are given an integer array called nums, and an integer k. Your task is to return the k elements that appear most frequently in that array. You can return them in any order you like.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: For example, suppose I give you the array one, one, one, two, two, three, and k equals two. What would you return?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Okay, so one appears three times and two appears twice. Those are the two most frequent elements. So I would return one and two.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Before I start, let me ask a few clarifying questions. Can the array contain negative numbers?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, the array can contain any integers, positive or negative.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. And is it guaranteed that k is always valid? I mean, will k always be between one and the number of distinct elements in the array?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, k is always valid. You do not need to handle a case where k is larger than the number of unique elements.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What about ties? For instance, if two elements have the same frequency, how do I decide which one to include?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: The answer is guaranteed to be unique, so you will never have an ambiguous tie that affects the result.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: And what if k equals one and all elements are the same? For example, the array is just five, five, five?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Then you would simply return that single element, which is five. That is a valid scenario.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Alright, let me summarize. I have an integer array and a number k. I need to find which elements appear most often and return the top k of them. The answer is always unique, k is always valid, and I can return the result in any order. Let me think about how to approach this.

sections.title: Sort by Frequency
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Build frequency map"] --> B["Collect unique elements"]
    B --> C["Sort by frequency descending"]
    C --> D["Take first k elements"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#2563eb,color:#fff
    style B fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#2563eb,color:#fff
    style C fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#2563eb,color:#fff
    style D fill:#60a5fa,stroke:#2563eb,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first thought is a straightforward approach. I will iterate through the array and build a hash map to count the frequency of each element.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Once I have the frequency counts, I will collect all the unique elements into a list. Then I sort that list by frequency in descending order, so the most frequent elements come first.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Finally, I just take the first k elements from the sorted list and return them. That gives me the k most frequent elements.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That sounds reasonable. What is the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Building the hash map takes O of n time, where n is the length of the array. Sorting the unique elements takes O of n log n in the worst case, since there could be up to n unique elements. So the overall time complexity is O of n log n.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The space complexity is O of n because we store the frequency map and the list of unique elements.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good analysis. The sorting step dominates the time complexity. Can you think of a way to avoid sorting all the elements?

sections.title: Heap-Based Selection
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Build frequency map"] --> B["Create min-heap of size k"]
    B --> C["For each unique element"]
    C --> D{"Heap size less than k?"}
    D -- Yes --> E["Push element onto heap"]
    D -- No --> F{"Current freq greater than heap top?"}
    F -- Yes --> G["Pop min, push current"]
    F -- No --> H["Skip element"]
    E --> C
    G --> C
    H --> C
    C --> I["Heap contains top k elements"]
    style A fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#fff
    style C fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#fff
    style D fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#fff
    style E fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#fff
    style F fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#fff
    style G fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#fff
    style H fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#fff
    style I fill:#a78bfa,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Instead of sorting all elements, I can use a heap to find just the top k. The key insight is that I only need the k most frequent elements, not a full sorted order.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: First, I build the frequency map just like before. Then I create a min-heap that orders elements by their frequency. The min-heap will keep track of the k elements with the highest frequencies.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I iterate through the unique elements. For each one, I push it onto the heap. If the heap size exceeds k, I pop the element with the smallest frequency. This way, the heap always contains the top k most frequent elements seen so far.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Why a min-heap instead of a max-heap?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Great question. With a min-heap, the element with the lowest frequency is always on top. When the heap exceeds size k, I pop the smallest. That guarantees the k elements remaining are the ones with the highest frequencies. If I used a max-heap, I would have to pop k times at the end, which would not improve the complexity.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The time complexity improves to O of n log k. Building the map is O of n. For each of the at most n unique elements, the heap push and pop operations each take O of log k. Since k is typically much smaller than n, this is better than O of n log n.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The space complexity is still O of n for the frequency map, plus O of k for the heap.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice improvement. But can we do even better and solve it in linear time?

sections.title: Bucket Sort Approach
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Build frequency map"] --> B["Create bucket array of size n plus one"]
    B --> C["Place each element in bucket at index equal to its frequency"]
    C --> D["Walk buckets from highest index down"]
    D --> E["Collect elements until k are gathered"]
    E --> F["Return result"]
    style A fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#fff
    style B fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#fff
    style C fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#fff
    style D fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#fff
    style E fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#fff
    style F fill:#fb923c,stroke:#ea580c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Yes, we can achieve O of n time using a technique called bucket sort. Here is the idea. The maximum possible frequency of any element is n, the length of the array. So I create an array of buckets with indices from zero to n.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: First, I build the frequency map as usual. Then, for each entry in the map, I place the element into the bucket at the index matching its frequency. For example, if the number seven appears three times, I add seven to bucket three.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each bucket is a list because multiple elements could share the same frequency. After filling the buckets, I walk from the highest index down to the lowest, collecting elements. I stop as soon as I have gathered k elements.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can you walk through the example? Given the array one, one, one, two, two, three, and k equals two.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. The frequency map is: one maps to three, two maps to two, and three maps to one. The array length is six, so I create seven buckets, indexed zero through six.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I place three in bucket one because three appears once. I place two in bucket two because two appears twice. I place one in bucket three because one appears three times. Buckets four, five, and six are empty.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Now I walk from the highest index. Buckets six, five, and four are empty. Bucket three contains one, so I add it to my result. Bucket two contains two, so I add it. I now have two elements, which equals k, so I stop and return one and two.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Excellent. What are the time and space complexities?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The time complexity is O of n. Building the frequency map is O of n. Creating and filling the buckets is O of n. Walking the buckets is also O of n in the worst case. So every step is linear.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The space complexity is O of n because we use a frequency map of up to n entries and a bucket array of size n plus one.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: This is a clever use of the constraint that frequencies are bounded by n. Well done.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Let's review the three approaches we discussed for finding the k most frequent elements.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The first approach was sort by frequency. We build a frequency map, sort the unique elements by count, and pick the top k. This runs in O of n log n time and O of n space. It is simple but the sorting step is the bottleneck.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The second approach used a min-heap of size k. We still build the frequency map, but instead of sorting everything, we maintain a heap that keeps only the top k elements. This improves the time to O of n log k, which is better when k is much smaller than n.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The optimal approach uses bucket sort. We exploit the fact that the maximum frequency is at most n. By creating buckets indexed by frequency and walking from highest to lowest, we achieve O of n time. All three approaches use O of n space.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great summary. The bucket sort approach is the best here because it achieves linear time. The key insight is recognizing that frequencies are bounded by the array length, which lets us avoid comparison-based sorting entirely.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Exactly. And in a real interview, mentioning all three approaches demonstrates a strong understanding of the trade-offs between sorting, heaps, and bucket-based techniques.
